frictionVectors.title: European Gas Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains strong state control over hydrocarbons, but European demand, pricing, and investment decisions continue to shape export revenues and infrastructure priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Southern Security Belt
frictionVectors.details: Instability in Mali, Libya, and Niger increases border-security costs and complicates Algeria's effort to preserve strategic autonomy in the Sahel.

frictionVectors.title: Lobito Corridor Competition
frictionVectors.details: US and European support for the Lobito Corridor is expanding Angola's infrastructure options, while China seeks to retain influence over logistics, minerals, and construction networks.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Oil Ecosystem
frictionVectors.details: Declining production and reliance on international operators constrain Luanda's bargaining power, despite state ownership and efforts to diversify beyond crude exports.

frictionVectors.title: Niger Pipeline Dispute
frictionVectors.details: The cross-border oil-export relationship with Niger remains vulnerable to political disputes, exposing Benin's port and pipeline infrastructure to regional pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Northern Border Insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Jihadist activity moving south from Burkina Faso and Niger threatens transport corridors and may increase reliance on external security assistance.

frictionVectors.title: De Beers Market Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Botswana has strengthened its position in the Debswana partnership, but diamond-price weakness and dependence on external marketing networks still limit full value-chain sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral Infrastructure Gap
frictionVectors.details: Prospective copper, nickel, and other critical-mineral projects face transport and energy constraints that could increase dependence on foreign capital and regional corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-Sector Rebalancing
frictionVectors.details: The junta is seeking greater state control over gold production and foreign mining concessions, but opaque contracting and insecurity complicate effective sovereign management.

frictionVectors.title: External Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Ouagadougou's growing reliance on Russian-linked security support reflects frustration with Western partners while creating new risks of political and resource leverage by Moscow-aligned actors.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals governance
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking greater control and revenue from nickel, gold, and rare-earth projects, but limited processing capacity leaves it dependent on foreign investors and export infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda border mistrust
frictionVectors.details: Relations with Rwanda remain strained over armed-group accusations and border security, complicating trade, transport, and regional resource coordination.

frictionVectors.title: Port and maritime competition
frictionVectors.details: Cabo Verde is leveraging its ports, airfields, and maritime position, but infrastructure development remains reliant on European, Chinese, and other external capital.

frictionVectors.title: Illicit maritime flows
frictionVectors.details: Drug trafficking and illegal fishing test the country's limited surveillance capacity and create dependence on foreign maritime-security assistance.

highlights: Oil and gas sovereignty under pressure

frictionVectors.title: External control of hydrocarbons
frictionVectors.details: Foreign operators, creditors, and trading partners remain central to upstream investment, LNG operations, and export finance, limiting domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Separatist corridor insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in the Northwest and Southwest disrupts roads, agricultural supply chains, and proposed infrastructure corridors while increasing security dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-for-security dependence
frictionVectors.details: Russian security personnel and associated commercial networks retain major influence around gold and diamond areas, limiting transparent state control over extraction.

frictionVectors.title: Transport chokepoints
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on Cameroon’s Douala corridor and insecurity on internal roads constrain sovereign trade access and leave the country vulnerable to neighboring and external gatekeepers.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon dependence
frictionVectors.details: Oil remains the fiscal backbone, while foreign firms, export routes, and international lenders retain substantial leverage over production and revenue flows.

frictionVectors.title: Post-French security transition
frictionVectors.details: The drawdown or restructuring of French military ties creates uncertainty over border security and counterinsurgency capacity as N'Djamena explores more diversified partnerships.

frictionVectors.title: FRANCE–COMOROS SOVEREIGNTY DISPUTE
frictionVectors.details: France's control of Mayotte remains the central sovereignty dispute and limits coordinated maritime governance. The issue continues to shape migration, aid, and diplomatic relations.

frictionVectors.title: LIMITED MARITIME CAPACITY
frictionVectors.details: Comoros has limited capacity to police its exclusive economic zone and develop fisheries or offshore resources. External assistance improves surveillance but can also increase dependence on foreign partners.

frictionVectors.title: MINERALS AND CONTRACT LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: Cobalt, copper, coltan, and other strategic minerals attract intense competition among Chinese, Western, and regional actors. Weak enforcement and opaque contracting continue to limit the state's capture of resource value.

frictionVectors.title: EASTERN CONGO CONFLICT
frictionVectors.details: Armed-group activity and alleged cross-border support, particularly around North Kivu and Ituri, constrain Kinshasa's territorial control. Conflict also disrupts mining corridors and enables illicit mineral flows.

frictionVectors.title: HYDROCARBON DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: The economy and fiscal system remain heavily dependent on oil, leaving sovereignty vulnerable to price shocks and the bargaining power of international energy companies. Diversification and domestic value addition remain limited.

frictionVectors.title: CHINESE INFRASTRUCTURE FINANCE
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed infrastructure has expanded transport and industrial connectivity but increases exposure to debt, project opacity, and long-term commercial concessions. Brazzaville retains political control while facing constrained fiscal room.

frictionVectors.title: COCOA VALUE-CHAIN CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: Côte d'Ivoire is pursuing greater domestic processing and producer protection, but multinational buyers and volatile global prices still limit national control over the cocoa economy. Regulatory gains remain vulnerable to fiscal and market pressures.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND SECURITY DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Abidjan's port and transport corridors are strategic assets, yet their expansion relies heavily on foreign capital and technology. Spillover risks from Sahel instability continue to raise the cost of securing northern trade routes.

frictionVectors.title: BASES AND GREAT-POWER COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: U.S., Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military facilities provide revenue and security but make Djibouti a center of strategic rivalry. The government gains bargaining power while facing pressure to balance incompatible external interests.

frictionVectors.title: PORT DEBT AND CORRIDOR CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti's ports and logistics corridors are vital to Ethiopian trade and global shipping, but debt exposure and foreign-linked infrastructure contracts constrain national room for maneuver. Competition with neighboring ports further increases reliance on external capital.

frictionVectors.title: GERD and Nile allocation
frictionVectors.details: Egypt continues to oppose unilateral Ethiopian control over Nile flows and seeks a binding operating framework for the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam. The dispute remains tied to food security, water sovereignty, and wider Red Sea competition.

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: IMF-backed reforms and Gulf investment support fiscal stability but increase outside influence over strategic assets, including ports, logistics, and state-owned enterprises.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon dependence
frictionVectors.details: Declining mature oil fields and limited economic diversification leave sovereign revenue exposed to production and price shocks. International energy firms retain significant technical and commercial leverage over offshore projects.

frictionVectors.title: LNG and regional infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: The country is seeking to preserve LNG and gas-processing relevance through regional supply arrangements, but financing, feedstock access, and opaque governance constrain local control over value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea strategic competition
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's coastline and proximity to the Bab el-Mandeb give it growing geopolitical value as external powers compete over maritime access and security partnerships. Asmara remains highly cautious about surrendering basing or port autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-sector external leverage
frictionVectors.details: Gold and base-metal projects provide scarce foreign exchange but depend heavily on foreign capital, technology, and operators. Concentrated ownership and limited transparency reduce domestic capture of resource rents.

frictionVectors.title: Logistics and energy dependence
frictionVectors.details: Eswatini relies heavily on South African transport corridors, electricity markets, and customs connectivity, limiting its room for autonomous infrastructure policy. Regional disruptions can quickly affect fuel, food, and export security.

frictionVectors.title: Resource-sector concentration
frictionVectors.details: Sugar, forestry, and agro-processing remain important export anchors but are exposed to external market access, water stress, and foreign-linked ownership. Diversification is gradual and constrained by the small domestic market.

frictionVectors.title: Nile and downstream pressure
frictionVectors.details: The GERD strengthens Ethiopia's control over hydropower and seasonal water management, but Egypt and Sudan continue to seek binding safeguards on dam operations. The dispute remains a major risk to regional cooperation.

frictionVectors.title: Debt restructuring and strategic assets
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-exchange shortages, debt negotiations, and infrastructure financing needs increase leverage for external creditors and investors. Conflict-related insecurity and contested access to transport corridors further complicate sovereign control over resources.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic mining concessions
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking greater domestic value capture from manganese and other minerals while managing entrenched foreign operators and financing dependencies.

frictionVectors.title: Oil-sector fiscal control
frictionVectors.details: Efforts to renegotiate resource terms and expand state participation risk friction with international oil companies and creditors.

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Foreign fishing activity and weak enforcement continue to threaten coastal resource security and local livelihoods.

frictionVectors.title: Port and energy dependence
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on external financing and regional supply networks limits Banjul's leverage over port modernization, electricity, and trade infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: IMF and creditor constraints
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and IMF-linked reforms narrow fiscal room, including the state's ability to direct revenues from strategic commodities.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal mining and foreign operators
frictionVectors.details: Galamsey is damaging water systems and agricultural land, while foreign-linked mining networks complicate enforcement and local resource control.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou corridor control
frictionVectors.details: Rail, port, and mine development gives the state new bargaining power but also deepens dependence on Chinese and multinational capital for strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Transition and contract risk
frictionVectors.details: Political uncertainty and concentration of executive power may trigger disputes over mining licenses, revenue allocation, and the credibility of future contracts.

frictionVectors.title: Port and trade influence
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on foreign-backed port, transport, and logistics arrangements limits national control over trade gateways and customs revenue.

frictionVectors.title: Cashew and illicit-finance networks
frictionVectors.details: A narrow cashew export base and persistent narcotics-trafficking risks make the economy vulnerable to outside traders, criminal intermediaries, and political capture.

frictionVectors.title: External Debt Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Debt-service pressure and IMF-linked reforms narrow Nairobi's room to set independent infrastructure and energy policy. Chinese-financed projects remain politically sensitive even as Kenya diversifies toward Western, Gulf, and private capital.

frictionVectors.title: Mombasa and Lamu Corridors
frictionVectors.details: Competition among foreign-backed logistics and port projects affects Kenya's control over regional trade routes. Security risks in northern Kenya and along the Lamu corridor continue to raise costs and limit integration with Ethiopia and South Sudan.

frictionVectors.title: Highlands Water Project
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's water exports to South Africa provide essential revenue but make national finances and infrastructure planning dependent on a larger neighbor. Delays, cost overruns, and power-supply constraints complicate the next phase of the project.

frictionVectors.title: Customs and Textile Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's manufacturing and import access remain vulnerable to South African logistics and changing external trade preferences. Foreign-owned textile operations provide jobs but leave limited domestic control over value chains.

frictionVectors.title: Iron Ore Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Large mining concessions, especially in iron ore, dominate Liberia's export prospects while concentrating bargaining power in foreign operators. The government's challenge is to convert royalties, jobs, and infrastructure commitments into durable domestic capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Monrovia Port Influence
frictionVectors.details: The port is central to Liberia's trade and fiscal security, with foreign operators and investors shaping modernization priorities. Weak transport links and limited state capacity reduce Liberia's leverage over logistics and mineral exports.

frictionVectors.title: Competing Oil Gatekeepers
frictionVectors.details: Rival political and security networks continue to contest control over oil facilities, budgets, and the National Oil Corporation. Production remains vulnerable to blockades and bargaining among domestic factions backed by external sponsors.

frictionVectors.title: Mercenaries and Strategic Bases
frictionVectors.details: Turkish, Russian-linked, Egyptian, Emirati, and other foreign security relationships continue to shape Libya's military balance and infrastructure access. Their presence limits sovereign decision-making and increases the risk that energy assets become instruments of geopolitical competition.

frictionVectors.title: Nickel and Cobalt Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large foreign-backed mining projects dominate Madagascar's nickel and cobalt exports, leaving the state exposed to commodity prices, investor decisions, and external demand. Power shortages and weak transport infrastructure further reduce domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Land, Forest, and Rare-Earth Competition
frictionVectors.details: Foreign investment in mining, agriculture, and energy competes with local land rights and environmental protections. Illegal logging and informal extraction continue to erode state control over strategic natural assets.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Investment
frictionVectors.details: Malawi is courting foreign capital for uranium, rare earths and graphite, but weak bargaining capacity and limited domestic processing risk leaving value capture abroad.

frictionVectors.title: Power and Fertilizer Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Hydropower shortages and dependence on imported fuel and fertilizer constrain national resilience, while external lenders retain substantial influence over fiscal and infrastructure policy.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Contract Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The junta is seeking a larger state share of gold revenues and greater control over industrial mining, increasing tensions with foreign operators and investors.

frictionVectors.title: Security and Strategic Alignment
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on Russian-linked security assistance has reduced Western leverage but deepened dependence on an external security partner amid worsening insurgency and regional isolation.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Gas Governance
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project with Senegal offers major revenue potential, but cross-border governance, local-content limits and foreign operator dominance constrain Mauritania's control over the value chain.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral Logistics Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore and gold exports remain dependent on foreign capital, rail capacity and port infrastructure, leaving the economy exposed to commodity cycles and external financing conditions.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos and Diego Garcia
frictionVectors.details: The sovereignty settlement with the United Kingdom and the future operating framework for the Diego Garcia base remain central tests of Mauritius's control over its maritime territory.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Financial Influence
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius is expanding maritime and logistics ambitions, but competition among Indian, Chinese and Gulf interests, together with offshore-finance scrutiny, limits room for fully autonomous economic policy.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara Resource Politics
frictionVectors.details: Morocco's control of phosphate, fisheries and renewable projects in Western Sahara continues to generate legal and diplomatic friction with Algeria, the Polisario Front and parts of the European market.

frictionVectors.title: External Capital and Water Stress
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Gulf and European financing supports ports, rail and renewable infrastructure, while severe water scarcity could constrain the sovereignty gains offered by domestic energy and phosphate capacity.

highlights: LNG revival remains hostage to Cabo Delgado security

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado Insurgency
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity continues to constrain LNG development and force reliance on foreign security support. International energy companies retain substantial leverage over the timing and terms of project reactivation.

frictionVectors.title: External Infrastructure Finance
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Gulf, and Western investors compete for ports, gas, and transport corridors. Debt exposure and concession structures limit Maputo's bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Oil and Uranium Investment Terms
frictionVectors.details: New petroleum prospects and established uranium production are attracting major foreign firms. Namibia is seeking greater local value capture while avoiding delays caused by regulatory uncertainty.

frictionVectors.title: Green Hydrogen Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: European and Gulf-backed projects could expand industrial capacity but may leave Namibia dependent on external technology, finance, and export markets. Water use and land access remain politically sensitive.

highlights: Junta asserts resource sovereignty against Western partners
Security and sanctions constrain economic autonomy

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Mining Disputes
frictionVectors.details: Niamey is renegotiating relationships with foreign mining interests while using uranium and gold policy to signal sovereignty. Operational disruption and legal uncertainty threaten revenues and technical capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Reduced Western military engagement has increased reliance on Russian-linked security assistance. This may preserve regime autonomy but creates new dependency and has not eliminated jihadist pressure on transport and mining corridors.

highlights: Reform is rebuilding control over energy markets
Oil theft and infrastructure gaps erode sovereignty

frictionVectors.title: Oil Theft and Pipeline Insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Crude theft, sabotage, and aging infrastructure continue to reduce public revenue and weaken Nigeria's leverage over international operators. Security contracting and foreign technical dependence remain entrenched.

frictionVectors.title: Refining and Strategic Finance
frictionVectors.details: Domestic refining capacity offers a path toward greater energy autonomy, but financing, imported equipment, and opaque commercial arrangements give external creditors and investors significant influence.

highlights: State capacity is strong but regionally contested
Mineral networks expose Kigali to sovereignty costs

frictionVectors.title: Eastern DRC Mineral and Security Network
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda faces sustained accusations of supporting armed actors linked to mineral flows in eastern Congo, while Kigali cites border security concerns. Regional pressure threatens trade access and diplomatic legitimacy.

frictionVectors.title: External Aid and Technology Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Western aid, Gulf investment, and foreign technology support Rwanda's development and security model. These relationships provide leverage to outside partners despite Kigali's tight domestic control.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore hydrocarbons
frictionVectors.details: Exploration interest in disputed or underdeveloped offshore blocks has raised expectations, but São Tomé and Príncipe still lacks the bargaining power and technical capacity to control major projects independently.

frictionVectors.title: External infrastructure finance
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Portuguese, and other external partners remain important for ports, energy, and public infrastructure, creating financing dependence without a single dominant patron.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore project control
frictionVectors.details: New oil and gas revenues are increasing Senegal's fiscal leverage, but foreign operators, production-sharing contracts, and financing arrangements still constrain domestic control over the sector.

frictionVectors.title: Port and logistics competition
frictionVectors.details: Dakar's strategic infrastructure attracts European, Chinese, Turkish, and Gulf interest, giving Senegal options while intensifying competition over transport corridors and maritime influence.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign fishing access
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles depends on foreign fleets and investment in tuna fisheries, leaving enforcement, licensing revenue, and ecological sustainability vulnerable to external commercial pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic maritime partnerships
frictionVectors.details: Indian, Chinese, European, and Gulf engagement in ports, maritime security, and logistics expands national options but exposes the archipelago to great-power competition.

frictionVectors.title: Iron ore and mining dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale iron ore and other mineral projects are reviving exports, but foreign ownership, contract terms, and limited local processing keep much of the value chain outside Sierra Leone.

frictionVectors.title: Pepel port and rail leverage
frictionVectors.details: Mining-linked rail and port infrastructure is strategically important yet highly tied to external operators and commodity cycles, limiting the state's control over critical logistics.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign security dependence
frictionVectors.details: Somalia's federal government relies heavily on external military, financial, and diplomatic support while negotiating the difficult transfer of security responsibilities amid al-Shabaab's continued threat.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime resource competition
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Gulf states, and international energy firms are positioning around ports, maritime security, and potential offshore hydrocarbons, while federal-regional disputes complicate sovereign control of resources.

frictionVectors.title: Power and rail bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Electricity shortages, port congestion, and rail failures constrain domestic mineral processing and weaken sovereign control over export value chains.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: China, the United States, and European partners are competing for access to platinum-group metals, manganese, and other minerals, pressuring Pretoria to balance nonalignment with investment needs.

frictionVectors.title: Oil transit vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan's crude exports depend on pipelines and ports crossing conflict-affected Sudan, leaving revenues exposed to disruptions and external bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Elite and foreign competition
frictionVectors.details: Political fragmentation and armed rivalries limit state oversight of oil concessions, while neighboring states and international firms compete for influence over production and transport.

highlights: Ports and gold shape external leverage

frictionVectors.title: Gold war economy
frictionVectors.details: Competing armed authorities and foreign-linked trading networks capture gold revenues, reducing the prospects for unified fiscal control and transparent resource governance.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea access contest
frictionVectors.details: Port access, military relationships, and humanitarian corridors along the Red Sea are strategic pressure points for regional and extra-regional powers.

frictionVectors.title: LNG bargaining and security
frictionVectors.details: Negotiations over large offshore gas projects must balance state revenue, local benefits, and investor certainty while coastal security remains a concern.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed rail, port, and mining projects could improve sovereign leverage, but financing terms and export dependence may limit domestic value addition.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: Lomé's role as a logistics hub brings strategic revenue but also exposes Togo to foreign shipping, financing, and regional security interests.

frictionVectors.title: Phosphate-sector concentration
frictionVectors.details: State influence over phosphate resources is substantial, yet limited processing capacity and external market dependence constrain domestic capture of the value chain.

frictionVectors.title: EU migration-finance linkage
frictionVectors.details: European support on migration management gives Brussels significant leverage over Tunisian policy and budget priorities. Domestic opposition frames the relationship as sovereignty erosion.

frictionVectors.title: Energy import dependence
frictionVectors.details: Tunisia remains vulnerable to imported gas and electricity, particularly amid fiscal constraints and pressure to reform subsidies. Delayed renewable-energy investment limits near-term autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP geopolitical exposure
frictionVectors.details: The East African Crude Oil Pipeline ties Uganda's oil strategy to foreign operators, Tanzanian transit infrastructure, and external financing. Environmental and human-rights criticism continues to raise diplomatic and reputational costs.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other foreign lenders remain important to Uganda's transport and energy build-out. Debt-service obligations can narrow Kampala's room to negotiate local-content and revenue terms.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of copper value chains
frictionVectors.details: International mining companies retain major influence over investment, technology, and export channels. Zambia is pressing for greater domestic processing and fiscal capture as copper demand rises.

frictionVectors.title: Creditor and infrastructure leverage
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring has eased immediate pressure but leaves policy constrained by official creditors and private lenders. Rail, power, and logistics bottlenecks continue to limit Zambia's bargaining power with mining investors.

frictionVectors.title: Lithium and mineral-licensing pressure
frictionVectors.details: Foreign investors, especially from China, are expanding roles in lithium and other strategic minerals. Harare is seeking beneficiation and tighter licensing while remaining dependent on external capital and technology.

frictionVectors.title: Sanctions and financial isolation
frictionVectors.details: Western sanctions and restricted access to conventional finance complicate infrastructure investment and reinforce reliance on alternative partners. Persistent currency instability further weakens the state's ability to capture and deploy mineral revenues.
